title: Landscape affects the community of fungal pathogens associated with Coraebus florentinus infestations in declining cork oak stands
content:
Abstract
Landscape and land-use are potential factors influencing the presence of insect pests and fungal pathogens, which can drive the onset of decline and mortality events. However, the impact of different types of landscapes on the community of insect-associated fungal pathogens still remains to be thoroughly understood. This study aimed to investigate the effect of landscape on plant-pathogenic fungi occurring in cork oak trees infested by Coraebus florentinus. Field surveys were conducted in 14 cork oak stands in Sardinia (Italy), classified as forest or woodland on the basis of the tree cover density. Fungi were isolated from wood materials sampled across various compartments of the gallery systems excavated by mature larvae of C. florentinus and identified based on morphological characteristics and DNA sequence analyses. Differences in fungal diversity between landscapes, as well as between gallery compartments and wood material types, were evaluated using ecological diversity indices and both non-parametric and ordination statistical methods. A total of 172 fungal isolates belonging to fourteen families and 26 species were obtained. Fungi in the Botryosphaeriaceae (41.28%), Nectriaceae (15.12%) and Cryphonectriaceae (12.79%) were the fungal families most frequently isolated from the infested branches. Diplodia corticola was the most frequently isolated species, representing 24.5 and 40.6% of total isolations in the forest and woodland areas, respectively. Multivariate analyses indicated that the presence and frequency of plant-pathogenic fungi were significantly associated with the predominant landscape. Results from this study emphasizes the importance of considering landscape types to facilitate risk assessment of the presence and spread of pathogenic fungi such as D. corticola and other members of the Botryosphaeriaceae family mainly involved in oak decline.
